did_you_know.text: The psalm’s heading attributes it to the sons of Korah and indicates that it was intended for the chief musician. It also includes the phrase “according to the Gittith,” whose precise meaning is not explained in the psalm itself.
The psalm opens with the words, “How lovely are your dwelling places,” expressing deep love for the LORD’s dwelling places, in the plural.
The poet describes his longing for the LORD’s courts and says that this longing encompasses his soul, heart, and body. In this way, the psalm portrays a desire that embraces the whole person.
The bird and the sparrow are used in the psalm as images of a home and nest beside the LORD’s altars. This picture emphasizes the longing for a place of permanence, shelter, and belonging.
The psalm calls those who dwell in the LORD’s house blessed and adds that they continue to praise him always: “They will still be praising you. Selah.”

Blessedness is also attributed to the person whose strength is in the LORD and whose heart is set on “highways” or “paths.” In other words, a relationship with the LORD is presented as a source of strength and inner direction.

Even those who pass through the Valley of Baca are described as being able to transform the journey into a place of springs and blessings. The verse presents the struggle along the way as a process that can bring blessing.

Those traveling the road go “from strength to strength” and ultimately appear before God in Zion. In this way, the psalm connects perseverance on the journey with reaching the place of encounter with the LORD.
In his prayer to the LORD God of hosts, the poet asks the LORD to hear his prayer, look upon his shield, and regard the face of his anointed one—the anointed king.
The psalm ends by declaring blessed the person who trusts in the LORD. This conclusion returns to the theme of happiness and presents trust in the LORD as the essence of the psalm’s message.
